“Little Marie,” he said to her as he sat down beside her, “I have come to cause thee pain and annoy thee, I know it well; but _the man and the woman of our house_ (thus designating, according to custom, the heads of the family) want me to speak to thee and ask thee to marry me. Thou dost not want to, I expect as much.”

“Germain,” little Marie replied, “is it settled, then, that you love me?”

“It angers thee, I know, but it is not my fault. If thou couldst change thy mind, I should be only too happy, and no doubt I do not deserve that it should be so. Come, look at me, Marie; am I really so frightful?”

“No, Germain,” she replied with a smile, “you are handsomer than I am.”

“Do not mock me; look at me indulgently. I have not yet lost either a hair or a tooth. My eyes tell thee that I love thee. Look into my eyes, then; it is written there, and every girl knows how to read that kind of writing.”

Marie looked into Germain’s eyes with her playful assurance; then, all at once, she turned her head away and began to tremble.

“Ah, my God! I frighten thee,” said Germain. “Thou lookest at me as though I were the farmer of Les Ormeaux. Do not fear me, I beg thee; it hurts me too much. I shall not say wicked things to thee, not I; I shall not kiss thee against thy will, and when thou wantest me to go away, thou needst only show me the door. Come, must I go out so that thou wilt stop trembling?”

Marie held out her hand to the plowman, but without turning her head away from where it was bowed toward the hearth, and without saying a word.

“I understand,” said Germain. “Thou pitiest me, for thou art good; thou art sorry to make me unhappy. But still, thou canst not love me?”

“Why do you say such things to me, Germain?” little Marie replied at last. “Do you mean to make me cry?”

“Poor little girl, thou hast a good heart, I know; but thou dost not love me, and thou hidest thy face from me because thou art afraid to let me see thy displeasure and thy repugnance. And I do not even dare to clasp thy hand! In the woods, when my son was asleep and thou wert asleep too, I nearly kissed thee very softly. But I would have died of shame rather than ask it of thee, and I suffered as much that night as a man who was being burned over a slow fire. Since then, I have dreamed of thee every night. Ah, how I kissed thee, Marie! But thou, all that time, wert sleeping without dreaming. And now, dost thou know what I think? It is that if thou wert to turn around and look at me with eyes like those I have for thee, and if thou wert to bring thy face close to mine, I believe I should fall down dead with joy. And thou, thou thinkest that if such a thing happened to thee, thou wouldst die of anger and shame!”

Germain spoke as though in a dream, without hearing what he was saying. Little Marie was still trembling; but as he was trembling even more, he no longer noticed it. All at once she turned around; she was in tears and looked at him reproachfully. The poor plowman thought this was the final blow, and, without waiting for her judgment, he rose to leave; but the young girl stopped him by putting both arms around him and, hiding her head against his breast, said to him between sobs:

“Ah, Germain, have you really not guessed that I love you?”

Germain would have gone mad if his son, who was looking for him and who came galloping into the cottage astride a stick, with his little sister riding behind him and whipping this imaginary steed with a willow switch, had not brought him back to himself. He lifted him in his arms and, placing him in those of his betrothed, said to her:

“Here, thou hast made more than one person happy by loving me!”






APPENDIX


I


THE COUNTRY WEDDING


Here ends the story of Germain’s marriage, just as he told it to me himself—the fine plowman that he is! I beg thy pardon, friendly reader, for not having known how to translate it better for thee; for the ancient and artless speech of the peasants of the region that I _sing_ (as they used to say in former times) truly requires translation. Those people speak too much French for us, and since Rabelais and Montaigne, the progress of the language has caused us to lose many old riches. So it is with all progress; one must resign oneself to it. Yet it is still a pleasure to hear these picturesque idioms prevailing upon the old soil of central France, all the more because they are the true expression of the mockingly placid and pleasantly fluent character of those who use them. Touraine has preserved a certain precious number of patriarchal turns of phrase. But Touraine became greatly civilized during and after the Renaissance. It became covered with châteaux, roads, foreigners, and activity. Berry has remained stationary, and I believe that, after Brittany and a few provinces in the extreme south of France, it is the most _preserved_ region to be found at the present time. Certain customs are so strange, so curious, that I hope to amuse thee for another moment, dear reader, if thou wilt allow me to recount in detail a country wedding—for example, Germain’s, which I had the pleasure of attending some years ago.

For alas! everything is passing away. Merely in the time that I have been alive, more change has taken place in the ideas and customs of my village than had been seen during the centuries before the Revolution. Already half of the Celtic, pagan, or medieval ceremonies that I still saw in full vigor in my childhood have vanished. Another year or two, perhaps, and the railways will carry their level across our deep valleys, bearing away, with the speed of lightning, our ancient traditions and our marvelous legends.

It was winter, around carnival time, the season of the year when it is fitting and proper among us to hold weddings. In summer there is scarcely time for them, and the work of a farm cannot suffer a delay of three days, not to mention the additional days devoted to the more or less laborious digestion of the moral and physical intoxication left behind by a celebration.—I was sitting beneath the vast hood of an ancient kitchen fireplace when pistol shots, the howling of dogs, and the shrill sounds of the bagpipe announced to me the approach of the betrothed couple. Soon Father and Mother Maurice, Germain and little Marie, followed by Jacques and his wife, their principal respective relatives, and the godfathers and godmothers of the betrothed couple, entered the courtyard.
